Last week you played a predator–prey game with candies and sticky notes.
Four things came out of it:

1. A simulation is a rule applied repeatedly, one step at a time.
2. Predation depended on *encounters* — the chance a fox and a rabbit met.
   That made the rate proportional to `R × F`.
3. A sealed meadow behaved nothing like an open one — immigration changed
   the model qualitatively, not just quantitatively.
4. Your step was one whole generation; a computer takes much smaller steps.

Today makes points 2, 3 and 4 precise.

## Block A — The law of mass action

**From encounters to collisions.** In the game, a rabbit died when a sticky
note landed on it: more rabbits → more caught per drop, more foxes → more
caught per turn, so catches per turn ∝ `R × F`. In a test tube, a molecule of
A reacts when it collides with a molecule of B: more A or more B means more
collisions, so reaction rate ∝ `[A] × [B]`. Same mathematics, different
reason for the motion — rabbits run, molecules diffuse.

**Waage & Guldberg, 1864.** The rate of a reaction is proportional to the
probability that the reactants collide, and that probability is proportional
to their concentrations, each raised to the power of the number in which it
enters the reaction (its molecularity). The commonest mistake in this course:
the exponents equal the stoichiometric coefficients *only* for elementary
(single-collision) reactions — an overall reaction as written in a textbook
is usually not elementary, and its rate law must be measured, not read off
the equation.

Why a *product*, not a sum: doubling `[A]` alone doubles the rate; doubling
both `[A]` and `[B]` quadruples it. A sum would only have doubled.

| Reaction | Molecularity | Rate law | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `∅ → A` | zero order | `v = k` | |
| `A → B` | first order | `v = k[A]` | |
| `A + B → C` | second order | `v = k[A][B]` | |
| `2A → B` | second order | `v = k[A]²` | dimerisation |

Units are a free error check: `v` is always concentration per time, so `k`
must supply whatever is missing.

**Worked example.** `A + B ⇌ C`: forward `v₊ = k₁[A][B]`, reverse `v₋ =
k₋₁[C]`, net `v = k₁[A][B] − k₋₁[C]`. At equilibrium `v = 0`, so `[C] /
([A][B]) = k₁/k₋₁ = K_eq` — the equilibrium constant is not an extra piece of
information, it's the ratio of the two rate constants. Thermodynamics and
kinetics are the same statement, read two ways.

## Block B — From a network graph to a system of ODEs

A reaction network is a graph: nodes are species whose amounts change, edges
are reactions, each edge carries one rate `v` written with mass action. The
equation for a species is nothing but the bookkeeping of the arrows that
touch its node.

**The recipe, every time:**

1. List the species — each gets an equation.
2. List the reactions — each gets a rate `v` from mass action.
3. For each species, add the rates of reactions that *produce* it and
   subtract those that *consume* it.
4. Multiply each rate by its stoichiometric coefficient.

Write down every rate `v` first; only then start writing `d/dt`. Mixing the
two steps is where almost every sign error comes from.

**Example 1 — closed, reversible:** `A ⇌ B`, forward `v₁ = k₁[A]`, reverse
`v₂ = k₂[B]`. The two right-hand sides are exact negatives, so
`d([A]+[B])/dt = 0` — `[A]+[B]` is constant. That's a conservation relation:
this two-variable system really has only one independent variable.

**Example 2 — the same network, opened up:** add `v₀ = k₀` (constant
influx). Now `[A]+[B]` is *not* constant.

| | Closed (ex. 1) | Open (ex. 2) |
|---|---|---|
| `[A] + [B]` | constant | not constant |
| Steady state | all net fluxes zero | fluxes constant, non-zero |
| Name | equilibrium | steady state |
| A living cell is… | | this one |

**The stoichiometric matrix.** One column per reaction, one row per species;
each entry is how many molecules that reaction makes (+) or consumes (−) for
that species. Every model in this course reduces to this matrix. Remember
this for meeting 4: a kinetic model solves `dx/dt = Sv(x)` for the
concentrations `x`. Flux Balance Analysis *sets* `dx/dt = 0` and solves
`Sv = 0` for the fluxes `v` — same matrix, different unknown.

## Block C — Open versus closed reaction networks

| | Closed → equilibrium | Open → steady state |
|---|---|---|
| Mass | conserved | flows in and out |
| At rest | every net flux = 0 | fluxes constant, not zero |
| Needs energy? | no | yes, continuously |
| Example | a sealed flask; a puddle | a chemostat; a river; a cell |

A cell at thermodynamic equilibrium is a dead cell — that's not a metaphor,
it's the definition. Every living cell continuously takes up substrate across
its boundary (the `k₀` terms), excretes product and waste (the `k₂` terms),
and maintains concentrations far from equilibrium at a cost in ATP. This is
why a genome-scale model has exchange reactions, and why its very first
constraint is a bound on glucose uptake — exactly the bound you'll set in
meeting 4.

## Block D — Simulating it in Python

**The five steps of any simulation**, and what last week's game called them:

| Step | In code | In the game |
|---|---|---|
| 1. State variables | `y0 = [1.0, 0.0]` | how many candies/notes to start with |
| 2. Parameters | `k1, k2 = 1.2, 0.4` | the rules card |
| 3. The model | `def rhs(t, y): ...` | the rules themselves |
| 4. Integrate | `solve_ivp(rhs, (0, 10), y0)` | playing the turns |
| 5. Plot | `plt.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0])` | drawing the graph |

Two code sketches walked through live: the **closed** system
(`dA/dt = -v, dB/dt = +v` with `v = k1*A - k2*B`) and the **open** one
(`dA/dt = k0 - k1*A, dB/dt = k1*A - k2*B`) — predict, before running, whether
`[A]+[B]` will be flat this time, then check the steady values analytically
(`A_ss = k0/k1`, `B_ss = k0/k2`) against the plot.

**What the solver is really doing.** Euler's method is the whole algorithm
in three lines: `y = y + dt*dy` inside a loop over fixed steps. That loop
*is* last week's game — one pass is one turn, `dt` is one generation, `dy` is
the rules card. Run it at `dt = 0.5, 0.1, 0.01` and overlay against
`solve_ivp` to see it converge.

**The five errors you will hit:**

| Symptom | Almost always |
|---|---|
| The curve is a flat line at zero | You returned the new values instead of the derivatives |
| Concentrations go negative | A sign error in the rhs, or a step size far too large |
| "could not broadcast" / shape error | `rhs` returned a list of the wrong length |
| The total drifts in a closed system | The two derivatives are not exact negatives |
| It runs forever | A stiff system — pass `method='Radau'` or `'BDF'` |

Read the last line of the traceback first, not the first — it's the one that
names your own function.
